title: AWS Backup & Snapshot Management
summary: Centralized, policy-driven backups with cross-Region, cross-account and immutable vaults.
tldr: **AWS Backup** centralizes backups for EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3 and more with **backup plans** (schedule, retention, lifecycle, copy rules) applied by tag.
Ransomware or "even an admin can't delete" → **Vault Lock in compliance mode**, plus copies to a vault in a **separate backup account** (or a **logically air-gapped vault**).
Organization-wide → **backup policies** in AWS Organizations. Cross-Region / cross-account → **copy rules** in the plan.
EBS snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs only, by tag, on a schedule → **Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM)** is the simpler native answer.

keyFacts.text: A **compliance-mode** Vault Lock can be changed only during its grace time (at least 3 days). After that nobody, not root and not AWS, can remove it or delete recovery points early.
**Governance-mode** locks can be removed by users with the right IAM permissions. They protect against accidents, not against a compromised admin.
Backups moved to **cold storage** must stay there at least 90 days. Use it for long-retention monthly or yearly backups that are rarely restored.
**Continuous backup** gives point-in-time restore for RDS, Aurora and S3 (up to 35 days). Combine it with snapshot rules for long retention.
**Restore testing plans** restore recovery points on a schedule, record restore time, and clean up afterward, proving backups actually work.

traps: RDS automated backups can't be kept for 7 years (maximum 35 days). Long retention needs AWS Backup or manual snapshots.
Deletion protection on RDS or DynamoDB stops the *resource* being deleted. It doesn't protect backups.
Governance mode is not enough when the requirement says *no one* can delete backups.
Copying backups to another vault in the **same** account doesn't survive an account compromise.
Don't replicate backup vaults with S3 CRR. AWS Backup storage isn't a bucket you control; use copy rules.
Audit Manager checks that resources *are* backed up. Restore testing checks that backups *can be restored*.
